newsitem.title: USA: Consumer media spending seen rising 6 percent in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Consumer media spending seen rising 6 percent in 1997.

text.p: Americans will spend an average of $546 this year on media and entertainment, ranging from movies to music to computer online services, up 6 percent from 1996, according to a survey released on Friday.

The same growth is expected next year, rising to an average of $583, and spending will increase to an estimated $685 by the year 2001, said media investment banking firm Veronis, Suhler & Associates Inc.

The biggest chunks of the 1997 pie so far are $156 for subscription television, $85 for books and $83 for home videos. Recorded music followed at $59, daily newspapers at $52, magazines at $37, computer online services at $27, movies at $26, video games at $17 and computer software at $4.
In all, consumer spending, which totalled $103.2 billion in 1996, is forecast to rise to $144.8 billion in 2001.

"Our forecast for sustained economic growth suggests a continuation in the strong performance of the communications industry over the next five years," Veronis said in its 11th annual Communications Industry Forecast.

Media consumption will outstrip economic growth, continuing a trend established after the World War II, said co-founder John Suhler. Communications as a percentage of gross domestic product will rise to 4 percent next year from 3.8 percent in 1996.
Computer online services will be a hot area next year, with spending rising 31 percent.
Total consumer spending for online services will grow to $10.2 billion by 2001, from $4 billion in 1996, while online advertising will shoot up to $2.5 billion from $200 million, Veronis said.

The company noted that consumer online growth is tied to how many households buy personal computers. While household penetration may be nearing its potential, increased Internet use should fuel demand for PCs.
The firm expects the number of U.S. computer households to rise to 45.1 percent by 2001 from 38.1 percent in 1996.

Spending for subscription video services -- which include direct broadcast satellite, basic cable and pay-per-view -- is forecast to rise 11 percent next year, and will surge 62 percent by 2001, to $55.5 billion, including advertising.

"Cable TV continues to grow faster than one would think," said Suhler. "Cable is adding footprints in the form of penetration." Total spending in basic cable TV alone will grow 11 percent this year from $20.3 billion in 1996, and to $30.9 billion by 2001.
Media and entertainment, which ranked 8th in total spending among the 12 largest U.S. industries in 1996, is expected to rise to third place by the year 2001.
Aside from consumer spending, the report forecast advertising expenditures will rise from $113.7 billion in 1996 to $165.6 billion by 2001.

Other big gainers will be business magazines and trade shows, which will rise 53 percent between 1996 and the 2001 to about $23 billion, and professional and educational publishing, forecast to rise to $35.5 billion by 2001 from $24.1 billion in 1996.
The firm produced the inch-thick report after analysing a mass of government and industry data, Veronis said.
